title: Writing messages
goal: Write messages and short letters in Georgian using everything you've collected — and close this book with a complete text you write yourself.
bekal: write a short letter with the right opening and closing
use the abbreviations Georgians use when typing
close the book by writing five sentences about yourself

dialogs.title: დიალოგი — A conversation on screen
dialogs.intro: This time it's not a spoken dialogue, but the messages Ani and Nino send each other over one day. Everyday written Georgian is shorter than the spoken language — notice which words get dropped.

lines.speaker: ანი:
lines.id: Hi! Good, you? I'm a bit busy.
lines.literal: hello! well, you? busy — I-am — a-little.

lines.speaker: ნინო:
lines.id: I'll be a bit late, sorry! I'll be there in ten minutes.
lines.literal: a-little — I-will-be-late, sorry! ten — minute-in — I-will-be.

lines.speaker: ნინო:
lines.id: What a lovely evening! Thank you!

lines.speaker: ანი:
lines.id: I really enjoyed it too. I'll call you tomorrow!

notes: **კაი is a shortened კარგი**, and it's almost never written in formal language — but it's in every typed conversation. It's like "ok" or "cool" in English. Don't use it in a job application.
**Numbers are typed as digits, not words.** *6 საათზე*, *10 წუთში*. A big relief for beginners: you don't have to spell out ოცდაათი when you're in a hurry.

**გელოდები = "I'm waiting for you".** Notice the prefix **გ-**, which means "you" as the object, just like in **გ**ქვია and **და**გ**ირეკავ** (I'll call you). Georgian packs two people into a single verb — and that's what makes its sentences so short.
**ხვალამდე! = "see you tomorrow!"** The -მდე ending from unit 11. Its partners: **შაბათამდე** (see you Saturday), **მოგვიანებით** (later).

**Georgians type in the Georgian alphabet, almost without exception.** Latin transliteration (*gamarjoba*) is used only when a keyboard has no Georgian letters, and less and less often. If you want to be taken seriously as a learner, install a Georgian keyboard on your phone today — the layout follows the sounds, so the "a" key types ა and "b" types ბ.

**Emoji are used the same way as anywhere else**, but one habit is different: Georgian text messages rarely open with long pleasantries. *გამარჯობა, როგორ ხარ?* is enough, followed straight away by the point.
**In written messages, pronouns are almost always dropped** — just as you've learned since unit 1. *დაკავებული ვარ* without მე, *ვნახოთ იქ* without ჩვენ. The shorter, the more natural.

grammars.title: A short letter: a template that always works
body: Formal letters and long messages in Georgia use the same template. Fill in the middle with sentences you already have.

rogor khar? didi khania ar ginakhivar
How are you? It's been a long time.
ახლა თბილისში ვცხოვრობ და ქართულს ვსწავლობ.
I live in Tbilisi now and I'm learning Georgian.
I hope we'll see each other soon.

after: **იმედი მაქვს** (I hope) is one of the most useful phrases for closing anything: *იმედი მაქვს, მალე შევხვდებით* — I hope we'll see each other soon.

grammars.title: Greetings and wishes
after: Notice the prefixes **გი-** and **გ-** in almost all of these wishes: once again, "to you" is already built into the verb. It's the same pattern you met in unit 1 in რა **გ**ქვია.

sections.title: Final exercise: write five sentences about yourself

blocks.text: This is the last exercise in the book, and the most important one. Write five sentences about yourself in the Georgian alphabet — not in your head, but actually written, on paper or on your phone. Everything you need is already in the twenty units behind you; you don't need a single new word.

head: Sentence
Taken from unit
Example
rows: Your name and where you're from
მე ბუდი ვარ. ინდონეზიიდან ვარ, ჯაკარტიდან.
Your job or what you do
ორი და მყავს და ერთი ძმა.
ხინკალი ძალიან მიყვარს, მაგრამ ღორის ხორცს არ ვჭამ.
მალე კახეთში წავალ. იმედი მაქვს, ქართულს კარგად ვისწავლი.

blocks.title: After you write it
items: **Read it out loud.** If you stumble over a word, that's a word you don't fully own yet — go back to its unit for a moment.
**Send it to someone.** A teacher, a Georgian friend, a study group. Sentences that someone else reads stick far better than sentences that sit in a notebook.
**Note the date.** Write the same five sentences again three months from now. The difference will surprise you, and it's the only measure of progress that can't lie.

blocks.text: And that's the end of these twenty units. You started with thirty-three letters that looked like random curls, and now you can read signs, order dinner, tell the story of your weekend, and turn down a glass of wine without offending anyone. That's no small achievement for a language unrelated to any other language you've ever heard.

The last sentence of this book is one you should say out loud, because you'll need it often: **ქართულს ვსწავლობ და ძალიან მიყვარს.** — I'm learning Georgian, and I love it. In Georgia, that sentence will open more doors than any passport.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
Translate into Georgian — the last five sentences of this book.
items: Thank you, what a lovely evening!
I hope we'll see each other soon.
I'm learning Georgian and I love it.

answers: ცოტა დაკავებული ვარ. — საღამოს კაფეში წავიდეთ. — ათ წუთში ვიქნები. — ხვალ დაგირეკავ. — იმედი მაქვს, მალე შევხვდებით.
გამარჯობა! როგორ ხარ? — საღამოს თავისუფალი ხარ? — არა უშავს, გელოდები. — მადლობა, ძალიან კარგი საღამო იყო! — იმედი მაქვს, მალე შევხვდებით. — ქართულს ვსწავლობ და ძალიან მიყვარს.
wave: Final spaced review: open unit 1 one more time, cover the pronunciation column, and read the dialogue from start to finish. If you can read it without stopping, you've arrived where the first page of this book promised.
